title: Eight Tips for Using the New Editing Practice that Sticks
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Guest author Doug Stark, writing to accompany the launch of Editing Practice that Sticks, offers eight practical tips for implementing the new resource in a secondary ELA classroom. He walks through routines for distributing a punctuation handbook, opening each unit with direct instruction and timed guided-notes practice, and using randomized cold-calling via index cards to keep students accountable, and describes choosing between quickwrites and focus-area checklists depending on whether students are editing a fresh exercise or an existing piece of writing. Stark also explains how to scale the checklists for group work on longer essays, sequence self-editing before peer editing, and adapt the comprehensive checklists to whichever error patterns are currently tripping up a given class. He closes by emphasizing flexibility — the materials are tools to mix, match, and adapt, not a rigid program — and states his underlying goal of saving teachers time while building genuinely better student editors.
points: Stark's core structure pairs brief direct instruction on a punctuation rule with an immediate, timed practice exercise and partner comparison, rather than isolated grammar drills.
Randomized cold-calling via index cards ("THIS STEP IS ESSENTIAL") is used deliberately to keep every student accountable for producing an answer, not just volunteers.
The checklists are designed to be applied directly to students' current writing assignments, not just to the exercises, so that editing skills transfer to real work.
Stark recommends self-editing before peer-editing as a sequencing default, adjusting the split across days depending on the length of the assignment.
quotes: What follows is a list of eight tips that Doug Stark has written for guiding teachers to use these exercises to the greatest effect possible.

I use index cards with student names on them to randomly choose students to call on. THIS STEP IS ESSENTIAL. Students learn very quickly that they will be called on, and they will have to provide an answer.
Directly connecting these activities to student writing is essential if you want to see carryover from the exercises to the students' actual work.
The basic purpose of these activities is to train the students to be active, engaged editors of text.
I always try to have students self-edit prior to peer editing. Depending on the length of the assignment and the time available, I will adjust my processes.

My goal in creating these editing books is to SAVE TEACHERS TIME. If these activities make it easier for you to quickly and efficiently teach kids how to become better writers, then I will be a very happy man.
